title: Understanding Backgammon
text:
What is this?
This is my notes for better understanding backgammon. I don’t expect anybody to ever stumble on this, but if you do, I hope you enjoy what you find, and don’t mind that this will be an unfinished project – at least for some time to come.

title: How we do this
text:
Backgammon decisions split more or less naturally into “positional” and “technical” problems.
The positional decisions require vision: Game plan, structural patterns, importance of points – all the more qualitative stuff.
Technical decisions, on the other hand, require counting: Shots, rolls and pips – the quantitative stuff.
Both types of positions, positional and technical, of course have both checker plays and cube plays (double and take decisions). So all in all we have four broad categories. Within those we focus on concepts for checker plays (splitting, hitting loose, etc).
For cube decisions we try find typical positions for: a) a minimal double, b) a solid double and solid take, c) a minimal take.
Let’s go.

title: Cube plays
text:
Attacking
Fairly common type of middle game position with attacking potential. Left, about the minimal strength that White would need to double; right, a variation that gives Black a minimal take.
Note the two significant changes: White got another powerful builder, Black moved a pip back so he can’t as easily anchor the 22-point.

title: Checker plays
text:
Bearoff

Deadly hits
So, you manged to close out two checkers, made it to the bear-off – this is about as good as it gets in backgammon. Still, even though the game feels like won, the occational surprise win is more common than many realize. Especially if you’re facing a strong enemy home board.
When to risk a deadly hit from the the bar in those situations? Not surprisingly your appetite for risk, shouldn’t be too great when loss is high. Still, some risk is in order, when it raises gammon (or backgammon) chances.
Consider:



A small risk is worth it











Analysis



Analyzed in Rollout, 6480 games at 2-ply

1. 6/off      eq: +1.289  ±0.001
   Player:   94.0% (G:42.4% B:1.2%)
   Opponent: 6.0% (G:0.0% B:0.0%)

2. 6/2 5/3    eq: +1.265 (-0.024)  ±0.001
   Player:   95.6% (G:36.3% B:0.8%)
   Opponent: 4.4% (G:0.0% B:0.0%)

3. 5/3 4/off  eq: +1.170 (-0.119)  ±0.001
   Player:   89.9% (G:40.3% B:1.1%)
   Opponent: 10.1% (G:0.0% B:0.0%)





A slightly higher risk is not











Analysis



Analyzed in Rollout, 6480 games at 2-ply

1. 6/2 5/3  eq: +1.295  ±0.001
   Player:   95.6% (G:39.2% B:0.9%)
   Opponent: 4.4% (G:0.0% B:0.0%)

2. 6/4 5/1  eq: +1.258 (-0.037)  ±0.001
   Player:   94.7% (G:37.8% B:0.9%)
   Opponent: 5.3% (G:0.0% B:0.0%)

3. 6/off    eq: +1.241 (-0.054)  ±0.002
   Player:   91.9% (G:42.7% B:1.3%)
   Opponent: 8.1% (G:0.0% B:0.0%)






Observations:

In both variations, the safe play is 6/2, 5/3 – that would be best at DMP.
The slightly risky play is 6/off – conceeding 55 and 66 as shot-leaving rolls
The risky play is worth it at the left hand side; sacrificing about a percentpoint of winning chances for some six percentagepoints extra gammon wins
At the right hand side the risky play is considerable more risky, sacrificing about 5 percentagepoints of wins, while gaining only 3 percentagepoints of extra gammon wins – not worth it.

The reason the risky play is too risky at the right hand side, despite the same 2/36 shot leaving rolls, is that quite a bit more rolls leads to trouble down the road: 65, 64, 63, 44, 33 are all much more problematic.
We can think of one or two shot leaving rolls as a ‘small’ risk. Some times a small risk comes not in the form of immediate shot-leaving rolls, but in the form of sacrificed flexibility. For example:



A flexibility risk worth it











Analysis



Analyzed in Rollout, 6480 games at 2-ply

1. 4/off    eq: +1.317  ±0.001
   Player:   95.1% (G:42.5% B:1.2%)
   Opponent: 4.9% (G:0.0% B:0.0%)

2. 6/3 5/4  eq: +1.291 (-0.026)  ±0.001
   Player:   96.8% (G:36.1% B:0.9%)
   Opponent: 3.2% (G:0.0% B:0.0%)

3. 6/2      eq: +1.244 (-0.073)  ±0.001
   Player:   93.9% (G:38.4% B:0.9%)
   Opponent: 6.1% (G:0.0% B:0.0%)





A flexibility risk not worth it











Analysis



Analyzed in Rollout, 6480 games at 2-ply

1. 6/4 6/3    eq: +1.244  ±0.001
   Player:   97.3% (G:30.5% B:0.6%)
   Opponent: 2.7% (G:0.0% B:0.0%)

2. 4/1 2/off  eq: +1.214 (-0.030)  ±0.001
   Player:   94.0% (G:35.4% B:0.6%)
   Opponent: 6.0% (G:0.0% B:0.0%)

3. 5/3 5/2    eq: +1.048 (-0.196)  ±0.001
   Player:   90.6% (G:26.0% B:0.4%)
   Opponent: 9.4% (G:0.0% B:0.0%)






In both positions White can bear off a checker at the expense of some flexibility, while conceeding no imediate shot-leaving numbers.
At the left the cost is about a percentagepoint of winning chances which is acceptable. At the right the inflexibility is more extreme and cost more than three times as much; not worth it.
Naturally, facing a weaker opposing board, the risk of leaving a shot is smaller, as a hit is surviable. So you get more inclined to leave those shots. For instance:



A shot and flexibility risk that breaks even

Here, bearing off is slightly risky, both in terms of imidiate and future shots. Left, the plays are about even, right, facing weaker opposition, bearing off is correct.
